quote: the consular authority was made annual, than that any diminution was made from the kingly prerogative
notes: Establishment of the free republic: annual consulship, popular oath against kings, senate filled to 300 with equestrians (conscripti).

quote: they might not be missed in any respect, they elect a king of the sacrifices
notes: A rex sacrificulus is created to perform former royal rites, subordinated to the pontiff to protect liberty.

quote: he resigned his consulship; and removing all his effects to Lavinium, he withdrew from the state
notes: Popular jealousy of the Tarquin name forces consul Collatinus to abdicate and withdraw; Brutus then carries a decree banishing the whole Tarquin family.

quote: when he perceived that they were given, he laid the whole affair before the consuls
notes: Spans cc.3-5: young nobles conspire with Tarquin ambassadors to restore the kings; a slave betrays the letters and the plot is crushed without tumult.

quote: After plundering the tyrants' effects, the traitors were condemned and capital punishment inflicted
notes: The conspirators, including Brutus's own sons, are condemned, scourged and beheaded under the father's consular supervision.

quote: a sum of money was granted out of the treasury as a reward to the discoverer; liberty also and the rights of citizenship were granted him
notes: The informer slave is freed and enfranchised, said to originate manumission by vindicta carrying citizenship.

quote: went round as a suppliant to the cities of Etruria, that they should not suffer him, sprung from themselves, of the same blood
notes: The exiled Tarquins solicit Veii and Tarquinii to restore them by force; resolved by the battle near the Arsian wood (c.6-7) where Brutus and Aruns die.

quote: the laws regarding an appeal to the people against the magistrates, and that devoting the life and property of any one who should form a design of assuming regal authority
notes: Spans cc.7-8: suspicion that Valerius aimed at kingship (house on the Velia) is answered by lowering the fasces, moving his house, and passing the appeal and anti-regal laws, earning him the name Poplicola.

quote: The friends of Valerius were more annoyed than they should have been, that the dedication of so celebrated a temple should be given to Horatius
notes: Partisan dispute over the dedication of the Capitoline temple; a false report of his son's death fails to deter Horatius, who completes the dedication.

quote: they advised him not to let this commencing practice of expelling kings pass unpunished
notes: Spans cc.9-15: the Tarquins persuade Porsena of Clusium to march on Rome; after siege, Mucius's attempt and embassies, peace is concluded and the restoration refused.

quote: Many conciliatory concessions were therefore granted to the people by the senate during that period
notes: Fearing the plebs might accept the Tarquins under siege conditions, the senate buys corn from the Volsci and Cumae, nationalizes the salt monopoly, and exempts the poor from port-duties and taxes.

quote: fled from Regillum to Rome, accompanied by a great number of clients. The rights of citizenship and land on the other side of the Anio were conferred on them
notes: Defeated in Sabine factional strife, Clausus migrates to Rome; citizenship and land granted, the 'old Claudian tribe' formed, and Appius enrolled in the senate.

quote: Among the oldest writers however I find that Titus Lartius was appointed the first dictator, and Spurius Cassius master of the horse
notes: Amid fear of the Latin confederacy (and distrust of consuls of Tarquinian faction) the dictatorship is created for the first time; the axes awe the commons into obedience.

quote: the colony which king Tarquin had sent to Signia was recruited by filling up the number of the colonists
notes: The royal colony at Signia is reinforced with new colonists.

quote: The tribes at Rome were increased to twenty-one
notes: Reorganization/expansion of the local tribes to twenty-one; same year patrician oppression of the plebs is said to begin after Tarquin's death.

quote: Those who were confined for debt, and those who were now at their liberty, hurry into the streets from all quarters and implore the protection of the people
notes: An aged centurion's display of debt-slavery scars ignites a city-wide tumult; the mob besets the senate-house and the consuls disagree, the crisis left hanging when Volscian invasion news arrives (span 23-24).

quote: They encouraged one another not to enrol their names, that it was better that all should perish together, than that they should perish alone
notes: Plebs refuse enrollment against the Volsci until Servilius's edict forbids detaining or seizing the property of soldiers for debt; the freed debtors then enlist eagerly.

quote: was transferred from the debtors to the creditors, who were severally abused by the crowd in the very sight of the consul
notes: After the war Appius enforces debt judgments with severity; crowds forcibly free debtors and intimidate creditors before the consul, decrees going unobeyed.

quote: The people gave the dedication of the temple to M. Laetorius, the centurion of the first legion
notes: The people, given the choice between the consuls, award the Mercury temple dedication to a mere senior centurion to affront the consuls and senate.

quote: the dread of the Sabine war spread, and when a levy was decreed, nobody gave in his name
notes: With debt grievances unredressed, no one enrolls for the decreed Sabine levy; Appius's attempt to seize a ringleader is defeated by appeal, and secret secessionist meetings begin.

quote: the consuls ascend the tribunal and summon the young men by name. But none of them made any answer
notes: Spans cc.28-29: plebs hold nightly meetings on the Esquiline and Aventine and refuse the levy until faith is kept; the consuls, berated by the senate, cannot enforce conscription.

quote: the riot was quelled by the interposition of the consuls, in which however, without stones or weapons, there was more noise and angry words than mischief done
notes: A crowd shields a summoned man, repulses the lictor and jostles the fathers; in the ensuing senate debate Appius proposes a dictatorship without appeal.

quote: They choose Manius Valerius, son of Volesus, dictator
notes: To meet sedition and triple war the senate appoints the moderate Manius Valerius dictator instead of Appius; his debt-protection edict induces the plebs to enlist ten legions.

quote: Then quitting the senate-house, he abdicated his dictatorship
notes: The senate, swayed by the money-lenders, rejects the dictator's motion for relief of debt-bondsmen; Valerius abdicates in protest and is applauded by the commons.

quote: colonists were sent from the city to Velitrae, and a colony planted there
notes: After the Volscian defeat the lands of Velitrae are confiscated and a Roman colony planted.

quote: they, by the advice of one Sicinius, retired, without the orders of the consuls, to the sacred mount, beyond the river Anio, three miles from the city
notes: Spans cc.32-33: the army, kept under arms by a pretext, secedes to the Sacred Mount (killing the consuls was first contemplated); Menenius's belly fable opens negotiation.

quote: Thus two tribunes of the commons were created, Caius Licinius and L. Albinus
notes: The settlement of the secession creates inviolable plebeian tribunes with power of aid against the consuls, closed to patricians; colleagues co-opted to five.

quote: first a scarcity of provisions, in consequence of the lands lying untilled during the secession of the commons; then a famine such as befals those who are besieged
notes: Famine follows the untilled fields of the secession; corn is sought from Etruria, Cumae (where ships are seized by Aristodemus) and Sicily, Etrurian corn sustaining the people.

quote: despatched a new colony to the mountains of Norba, to serve as a barrier in the Pomptine district
notes: Colonist numbers at Velitrae are augmented and a new colony sent to Norba as a frontier barrier.

quote: If they desire the former rate of provisions, let them restore to the senators their former rights
notes: Debate on pricing Sicilian relief corn: Coriolanus urges using the famine to abolish the tribunate; spans cc.34-35, provoking near-violence and his prosecution.

quote: Being condemned in his absence, he went into exile to the Volsci, threatening his country, and even then breathing all the resentment of an enemy
notes: The tribunes appoint Coriolanus a trial day, deflecting mob violence; condemned in absentia, he goes over to the Volsci and Attius Tullus.

quote: having pitched his camp at the Cluilian trenches five miles from the city, he from thence ravages the Roman territory
notes: Spans cc.35-40: the exile Coriolanus brings Volscian arms against Rome, sparing patrician lands; embassies and priests fail, but the matrons led by his mother Veturia induce withdrawal.

quote: Then, for the first time, the Agrarian law was proposed, which even down to our own recollection was never agitated without the greatest commotions in the state
notes: Cassius proposes dividing Hernican land and occupied public land among Latins and plebs; his colleague and senate resist, the plebs themselves distrust it, and the law fails.

quote: it is certain that he was condemned and put to death
notes: On leaving office Cassius is condemned for aiming at kingship—either by his father's domestic judgment or tried for treason by the quaestors—executed, and his house razed.

quote: In that year also the minds of the people were excited by the charms of the agrarian law
notes: Tribunes press the agrarian law after Cassius's death; senators and Fabian consuls resist and the law comes to nothing; soldiers also defrauded of booty by consul Fabius.

quote: Oppia, a vestal virgin, being found guilty of a breach of chastity, was made to suffer punishment
notes: Prodigies and divine anger are expiated by the trial and punishment of the Vestal Oppia for unchastity.

quote: Sp. Licinius, a tribune of the people, thinking that the time was come for forcing the agrarian law on the patricians
notes: Tribune Sp. Licinius obstructs the levy to extort the agrarian law; his own colleagues side with the consuls and the levy is completed.

quote: he routed the enemy's army solely by a charge of his cavalry, the infantry refused to pursue them when routed
notes: Out of hatred of consul Fabius the infantry refuse to pursue the beaten Aequi and return to camp without orders; no remedy is applied.

quote: It was Titus Pontificius: he pursuing the same course, as if it had succeeded with Sp. Licinius, obstructed the levy for a little time
notes: On Appius's advice the senate splits the tribunician college, and four tribunes against one enable the consuls to complete the levy.

quote: It is therefore resolved and determined not to give the signal, unless they swear that they will return victorious from this battle
notes: Spans cc.45-47: fearing a repeat of the army's willful defection, the consuls withhold battle until the soldiers voluntarily swear to return victorious; feared mutiny never materializes.

quote: that they should distribute among the commons the land taken from the enemy in as equal a proportion as possible
notes: Consul Kaeso Fabius urges the patricians to pre-empt the tribunes by distributing conquered land to the commons; the senate rejects the proposal with scorn.

quote: That war, as the property of our family, it is our determination to conduct at our own private expense
notes: The Fabian gens assumes the Veientine war as a private family undertaking; 306 Fabii march to the Cremera (c.49) and are annihilated (c.50).

quote: scarcity of provisions bearing hard upon them in addition to the war
notes: With the Etruscans holding the Janiculum after the Cremera disaster, scarcity of corn presses the city until the enemy is defeated; plenty returns with peace (c.52).

quote: Q. Considius and T. Genucius, the proposers of the agrarian law, appoint a day of trial for T. Menenius
notes: Menenius is tried for failing to relieve the Cremera fort, fined 2,000 asses despite senatorial pleas, and dies of the disgrace.

quote: Another senator, Sp. Servilius, being soon after arraigned, as soon as he went out of office, a day of trial having been appointed for him
notes: Servilius, charged over the Janiculum battle, defends himself boldly without supplication and escapes condemnation, aided by Menenius's fate and his colleague's testimony.

quote: Cn. Genucius, a tribune of the people, arraigned the consuls on their going out of office
notes: Ex-consuls Furius and Manlius are prosecuted for resisting the agrarian law; the trial collapses when the prosecuting tribune is found dead on the trial day.

quote: those who had been waiting before the gate of the tribune's residence, bring word that he was found dead in his house
notes: After secret patrician meetings resolved to rescue the accused 'by just or unjust means', tribune Genucius is found dead; patricians openly exult and no one is punished.

quote: the lictors being maltreated, the fasces broken, they are driven from the forum into the senate-house, uncertain how far Volero would push his victory
notes: During a cowed levy, ex-centurion Volero appeals against being enrolled as a common soldier; the crowd repulses the lictors, breaks the fasces and drives the consuls from the forum; elder senators counsel restraint.

quote: the contest would have ended in a battle, not without blood, had not Quintius, the other consul
notes: At the vote on Volero's law tribune Laetorius tries to remove the nobles, exchanges officers with consul Appius, and bloodshed is barely averted by Quintius's mediation.

quote: Overcome however by the unanimous feeling of the senators, he desisted: the law is carried without opposition
notes: Spans cc.55-58: Volero's law transfers election of plebeian magistrates to the tribal assembly, ending patrician influence through clients; five tribunes first so elected (c.58).

quote: they were not only unwilling to conquer, like Fabius' army, but they wished to be conquered
notes: Spans cc.58-59: the army, hating Appius, deliberately courts defeat and flees before the Volsci; Appius beheads arms-losers and standard-bearers and decimates the rest.

quote: as if a third consul, Marcus Duilius and Caius Sicinius appointed a day of trial
notes: Appius, chief opponent of the agrarian law and champion of the possessors, is put on trial; defiant and unbowed, he dies (of disease, per Livy) before the postponed trial day arrives.

quote: The commons appeared determined no longer to brook a delay of the agrarian law, and extreme violence was on the eve of being resorted to
notes: Sedition over the still-delayed agrarian law nears open violence but is checked by a Volscian incursion and the marching out of the youth.

quote: The exasperated commons refused to attend the consular elections: Titus Quintius, Quintus Servilius, were elected consuls by the patricians and their dependents
notes: The commons boycott the consular comitia; the patricians and their dependants elect the consuls alone.
